    tokio::select! is not cancellation‑safe by default: when one branch wins, all other futures are dropped immediately, and any cancel‑unsafe future (e.g., write_all, read_exact, Mutex::lock) may lose partial progress or corrupt state.

    What “Cancellation Safety” Means

    A future is cancel‑safe if dropping it at any .await point leaves the world consistent — no partial writes, no lost bytes, no corrupted buffers.
    A future is cancel‑unsafe if dropping it mid‑operation can lose progress or leave inconsistent state.
    Examples from Tokio’s documentation:

    • Safe: mpsc::Receiver::recv, sleep, TcpStream::readable Medium
    • Unsafe: AsyncWriteExt::write_all, AsyncReadExt::read_exact, tokio::sync::Mutex::lock Medium

    Why tokio::select! Is Dangerous

    select! races futures and drops all losing branches immediately.
    If a losing branch was performing cancel‑unsafe work (e.g., writing to a DB, reading into a buffer, locking a mutex), partial progress may be lost silently.
    Example:

    Rust
    tokio::select! {
        result = reader.read(&mut buf) => { /* may have partially filled buf */ }
        _ = tokio::time::sleep(timeout) => { /* timeout */ }
    }

    If sleep wins, the read future is dropped and any partially read bytes are lost. its-saeed.github.io

    Safe Patterns

    1. Use Cancellation‑Safe Alternatives

    Prefer operations documented as cancel‑safe:

    Rust
    tokio::select! {
        msg = rx.recv() => { /* safe */ }
        _ = token.cancelled() => { return; }
    }

    its-saeed.github.io

    2. Move Work Into a Spawned Task

    Spawn cancel‑unsafe work so it continues even if the select! branch loses:

    Rust
    let handle = tokio::spawn(async {
        writer.write_all(&data).await
    });

    tokio::select! {
        result = handle => { /* write completed */ }
        _ = shutdown => { /* write still continues */ }
    }

    its-saeed.github.io

    3. Pin and Reuse the Same Future

    Reusing a single future prevents losing partial progress when looping:

    Rust
    let mut fut = std::pin::pin!(reader.read(&mut buf));

    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            res = &mut fut => { /* safe: same future retains progress */ }
            _ = tokio::time::sleep(timeout) => { /* other branch */ }
        }
    }

    prachub.com

    4. Move Partial Progress Into Caller‑Owned State

    Track offsets or buffer state yourself so dropped futures don’t lose progress.
    This is essential for operations like read_exact. prachub.com

    Practical Guidance

    • Never put cancel‑unsafe futures directly inside select! unless you fully understand the consequences.
    • Audit async functions for cancel safety — Tokio marks many of them explicitly.
    • Use spawn for operations that must run to completion.
    • Use channels or other cancel‑safe primitives for coordination.
    • Avoid holding a Mutex across .await inside select! — dropping the future drops the lock attempt and may leave inconsistent state. Medium

    The core rule: select! cancels losing futures immediately, so only cancellation‑safe futures belong inside it.
